title: The Late Wardrobe
premise: Mara Oyelaran has spent seven years as a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, keeping her family at the polite distance of unanswered calls and almost-said truths about who she is and why she left. When her estranged grandmother dies and a stranger at the funeral greets the mourners by a name nobody uses anymore—the name Mara's mother abandoned when she fled the old neighborhood—Mara realizes the family story was never hers alone to keep hidden. Following the stranger's trail back to the condemned district before the last bus route is permanently rerouted, she uncovers a wardrobe of letters, photographs, and a second identity her grandmother lived openly for decades. In claiming that inheritance, Mara finally says what she has practiced not saying for seven years, choosing found family over silence as the old neighborhood—and its secrets—are demolished.
about_author: Tamsin Marchetti is a former night-shift archivist who writes novels about cities after midnight and the families we assemble in their margins. She lives above a shuttered laundromat with two cats named after bus routes.

chapters.title: The Hours Nobody Claims
chapters.summary: POV Mara. A night shift at the central library introduces Mara's ritualized invisibility—shelving returned books, avoiding the day staff, drafting texts to her sister she never sends. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Notice of Rerouting
chapters.summary: POV Mara. A transit notice announces the 47 bus line to the old neighborhood will be discontinued in six weeks; simultaneously, a call comes: her grandmother Iya Agnes is dead. Emotional beat: dread masquerading as indifference.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Knew
chapters.summary: POV Mara. At the funeral, a white man in an ill-fitting suit embraces the family and calls them by 'Oyelaran-Adeyemi,' a hyphenated name no one uses. Her aunt flinches; the stranger watches Mara specifically. Emotional beat: the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Flashback woven through the wake: seven years ago Mara left home after a fight with her mother over her transition and her refusal to come 'back to the church.' Emotional beat: grief braided with unfinished argument.

chapters.title: What the Aunt Burned
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Sorting the house, Mara finds a scorched tin where documents should be; her aunt Funke admits burning papers but swears some were already gone. The stranger's card sits in the doorframe mail slot. Emotional beat: suspicion kindling into purpose.

chapters.title: The Man Called Brother
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara tracks the stranger, Desmond, to a hostel; he claims to be Iya Agnes's ward from the neighborhood's vanished halfway house, raised under the double-barreled name. He mentions a wardrobe left to 'the one who stayed away.' Emotional beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: Last Bus Standing
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara rides the 47 one final evening before rerouting, watching the old district through the window—demolition crews, boarded storefronts, the halfway house now a fence. Emotional beat: mourning a place while it still stands.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe
chapters.summary: POV Mara. In the sealed back room of the old house, they find the wardrobe: inside, forty years of letters between Iya Agnes and a woman named Edith, plus adoption papers bearing Desmond's original name. Emotional beat: awe tipping into vertigo.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The letters reveal Iya Agnes's decades-long partnership with Edith, a white social worker who founded the halfway house—hidden from church and family alike. Mara recognizes her own concealment in her grandmother's. Emotional beat: inheritance reframed.

chapters.title: Funke's Version
chapters.summary: POV Funke. The aunt's perspective: she burned the letters years ago to protect her mother, believing secrecy was love, and resents Mara for leaving while she stayed and carried the weight. Emotional beat: resentment softening toward confession.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Desmond explains the double-barreled surname honored both women; the family dropped it after Edith's death. Mara tries the name aloud and it fits like a coat she never knew was tailored for her. Emotional beat: tentative self-recognition.

chapters.title: Day Staff
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Back at the library, Mara's daytime counterpart notices her distraction; a small kindness—a saved newspaper clipping about the demolition—cracks Mara's isolation. Emotional beat: the first offer of friendship accepted.

chapters.title: Mother on the Line
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara's mother calls demanding the house be sold quickly and the wardrobe forgotten; mid-argument, Mara almost says everything, then doesn't—but for the first time hears the silence as a choice, not a failure. Emotional beat: agency stirring.

chapters.title: Letters to Edith, Unsent
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Deeper in the wardrobe: drafts of letters Iya Agnes wrote to Mara herself, unsent, asking forgiveness for staying silent about Edith and urging Mara not to repeat it. Emotional beat: being seen across generations.

chapters.title: Desmond's Claim
chapters.summary: POV Desmond. His chapter reveals his stake: the will names him co-inheritor, but Funke contests it, and he needs Mara's testimony that the letters prove his belonging. Emotional beat: fear of being disowned twice.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Probate mediation turns hostile; Funke's lawyer paints Desmond as a fraud and Mara as a stranger to her own family. Mara must decide whether to speak. Emotional beat: rising pressure toward the unsayable.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: POV Mara. On the stand, Mara says all of it—her name, her leaving, her grandmother's Edith, Desmond's place in the family—in one unbroken breath. The room goes quiet; her mother walks out. Emotional beat: catharsis with a cost.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Breath
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The ruling grants Desmond half and Mara custody of the letters; her mother cuts contact, and Mara grieves the relationship honestly for the first time instead of practicing its loss. Emotional beat: sorrow without shame.

chapters.title: The Reading Room
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara proposes exhibiting the letters at the library; the day staff help build it, and neighbors from the old district contribute photographs of the halfway house. Emotional beat: found family assembling in public.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The neighborhood comes down; Mara, Desmond, and Funke watch from the last standing porch. Funke finally reads one of Edith's letters aloud and weeps. Emotional beat: collective release.

chapters.title: Oyelaran-Adeyemi
chapters.summary: POV Mara. At the exhibition opening, Mara introduces herself with the full double name; her sister arrives unannounced, takes her hand, and stays. Emotional beat: reconciliation earned, not granted.

chapters.title: First Bus of the New Route
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Months later, a new bus line serves the redeveloped district; Mara rides it at dawn with Desmond, carrying a letter she has finally written and sent to her mother—no answer needed yet. Emotional beat: open-ended hope.
